# What steady state misses {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Two different questions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Steady state**

*What does the aquifer settle down to if this pumping never changes?*

Useful. Not what anyone asks.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Transient**

*When does the water table reach the pump intake?*

*How much of what we pump this year is coming out of storage?*
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
The second set needs time in the model — and storage properties, which a
steady-state run does not even require you to supply.
:::

## Stress periods and time steps

::: {.incremental}
- A **stress period** is an interval over which every stress is constant.
  Change the pumping rate, you need a new period.
- A **time step** is a solver interval *within* a period. More steps means a
  better transient response and a slower run.
:::

```python
perlen = [1.0, 30.0] + [365.0] * 10     # length of each period
nstp   = [1,   30]   + [4] * 10         # steps within each
steady = [True] + [False] * 11          # one flag per period
```

## Your turn: read the discretization

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_time
perlen = [1.0, 30.0] + [365.0] * 10
nstp = [1, 30] + [4] * 10
steady = [True] + [False] * 11
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_time
n_periods = ______
n_steps = ______
simulated_days = ______
print(f"{n_periods} stress periods, {n_steps} time steps")
print(f"{simulated_days:,.0f} transient days = {simulated_days / 365:.1f} years")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_time"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The transient days are the `perlen` values whose `steady` flag is `False`.
`zip` pairs them up.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_time"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
n_periods = len(perlen)
n_steps = sum(nstp)
simulated_days = sum(p for p, s in zip(perlen, steady) if not s)
```

12 periods, 71 steps, 3,680 days — just over ten years.

**Note the odd 30-day period with daily steps.** The interesting part of a
transient response happens at the start, and a quarterly time step walks straight
over it. Fine early steps cost almost nothing.
:::
:::

## Resolve what you came to see

::: {.fragment}
Choosing time steps is the same problem as choosing cell size, and it has the same
answer: **finer than the feature you are trying to observe.**
:::

::: {.fragment}
A well switching on produces most of its head change in days. Sample it quarterly
and your hydrograph starts at the answer.
:::

# Storage {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Two properties, three orders of magnitude apart

| Property | Symbol | Applies when | Typical | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Specific yield** | `sy` | unconfined — pores drain | 0.05 – 0.30 | — |
| **Specific storage** | `ss` | confined — water expands, matrix compresses | 1e-6 – 1e-4 | 1/m |

::: {.fragment}
A confined aquifer releases almost no water per metre of decline. That is why
confined drawdown propagates so far, so fast.
:::

## Your turn: how much water is in there?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_storage
sy, ss = 0.15, 1e-5
cell_area = 250.0 * 250.0
thickness = 200.0
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_storage
unconfined = ______
confined = ______
print(f"released by 1 m of decline in one cell:")
print(f"  unconfined {unconfined:9,.1f} m3")
print(f"  confined   {confined:9,.1f} m3")
print(f"  ratio      {unconfined / confined:9,.0f}x")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_storage"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Specific yield is dimensionless — multiply by area alone. Specific *storage* is per
metre of aquifer, so it needs the thickness too.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_storage"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
unconfined = sy * cell_area
confined = ss * cell_area * thickness
```

9,375 m³ against 125 m³ — a factor of **75**.

The ratio is `sy / (ss × b)`, so it depends on thickness: a thin confined aquifer
is even more extreme. What it means is that **the same well drains an unconfined
aquifer over years and a confined one over days**, before either has to start
capturing flow from elsewhere.
:::
:::

## An upper bound worth computing

Across all 2,400 cells, 1 m of decline in our confined aquifer releases
**300,000 m³**.

::: {.fragment}
At 20,000 m³/d, that is **15 days** of pumping.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And that is an upper bound, because nothing like the whole aquifer drops a metre —
drawdown is concentrated near the well.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
So a confined aquifer reaches something close to steady state quickly. **The
Week 11 steady-state model was answering a question about the near future**, which
is worth knowing before you dismiss it.
:::

# The steady-state warm-up {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Why period 0 has no pumping

A transient model needs an initial head field. Any field you invent is **out of
equilibrium with the boundaries**.

::: {.incremental}
- So the model spends its first years relaxing toward balance
- And you cannot tell that artificial drift from the response you came to measure
:::

::: {.fragment}
Run one steady-state period first, with no pumping. Its heads are *already* in
equilibrium. Everything after that is the response to the stress you added.
:::

## Your turn: build the well schedule

The well is off in period 0 and pumps 20,000 m³/d from period 1 onward.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_schedule
NPER = 12
PUMP_RATE = 20000.0
WELL_LAY, WELL_ROW, WELL_COL = 0, 20, 30
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_schedule
wel_spd = {
    p: [[WELL_LAY, WELL_ROW, WELL_COL, ______]]
    for p in range(NPER)
}
print(f"period 0 rate: {wel_spd[0][0][3]:,.0f} m3/d")
print(f"period 1 rate: {wel_spd[1][0][3]:,.0f} m3/d")
print(f"periods defined: {len(wel_spd)}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_schedule"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

A conditional expression: zero if it's period 0, otherwise the negative pumping
rate. Remember negative means extraction.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_schedule"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
0.0 if p == 0 else -PUMP_RATE
```

Note that the dictionary has an entry for **every** period. If you skip one,
FloPy silently reuses the previous period's data — which is convenient when you
mean it and a very quiet bug when you don't.

Build these with a comprehension over `range(NPER)` and you cannot get it wrong.
:::
:::

What you did today
:::

- Steady state answers "what settles down to"; transient answers "when"
- Stress periods hold stresses constant; time steps subdivide them
- `sy` and `ss` differ by a factor of `sy / (ss·b)` — about 75 here
- 15 days of storage in a confined aquifer, as an upper bound
- Start every transient run with a no-pumping steady-state period
